input.question: Why are most orchestral pieces string dominated? And why are so many pieces written for that style of orchestra?
input.ground_truth: When brass instruments first came out they didn't have valves, so they could only hit a small variety of notes. This meant that all the melodies had to be carried by the strings, which were capable of hitting many more notes, and some like the Violin could even hit several octaves. There are some more recent pieces where the brass instruments are the ones carrying the melody, but I don't remember them off the top of my head.

Okay! Imagine you have a big box of toys, but most of them are different kinds of string toys—like rubber bands, jump ropes, and yarn. Now, when you want to make music with your friends, you find that these string toys make really pretty sounds and you can play them together in lots of different ways.

Long ago, people found that string instruments like violins, cellos, and harps make beautiful music and can play very softly or very loudly. They can also play fast or slow, and lots of notes at the same time. So, when people started making big groups of musicians (called orchestras), they used a lot of string instruments because they are so good at making music together.

That’s why most orchestral music is made for string instruments—they’re really flexible and sound nice together! And because so many people got used to hearing music made by strings, they kept writing music for them. It’s like having a favorite toy that everyone wants to play with!
